confusing.title: The pairs that cost marks in working-capital questions
rows: Gross working capital vs net working capital
Gross is the investment in current assets; net deducts current liabilities
'Gross' means before any deduction
Permanent vs temporary working capital
Permanent is the minimum carried at all times, financed long term; temporary meets sales fluctuation, financed short term
Does it disappear when sales fall back?
Finished goods vs debtors, on a cash-cost basis
Finished goods at the cash cost of **production**; debtors at the cash cost of **sales**
Has it passed the sales office yet?
W vs F in the operating cycle
W is divided by cost of production; F by cost of goods sold
The denominator is the cost flowing through that stage
'20% of working capital' vs '20% inclusive of the margin'
The first multiplies by 1.20; the second divides by 0.80
The word 'inclusive' is a gross-up instruction
Operating cycle vs cash cycle
The cycle splits inventory into R, W and F; the cash cycle takes inventory as one period
A cash cycle produces a minimum cash balance, not a working-capital figure
Baumol vs Miller-Orr
Baumol assumes certainty and gives one optimum; Miller-Orr assumes randomness and gives three limits
If the cash flow is stochastic it is Miller-Orr
Cheque processing float vs banking processing float
Processing runs from receipt to deposit; banking from deposit to credit
The moment of deposit divides them
Concentration banking vs lock box
Concentration banking uses the company's own regional centres; the lock box has the bank collect directly
Who opens the envelope?
Total Approach vs Incremental Approach
Total works in levels for every policy; Incremental works in differences
Does the statement show the present policy's own profit?
Factoring vs pledging
Factoring is a sale, so no debt; pledging is a loan secured on receivables, so debt rises
Does the debt-equity ratio move?
Factoring vs forfaiting
Factoring covers the sales ledger, may be with recourse, includes service; forfaiting is export bills only, always without recourse, finance alone
If it is an export bill under a letter of credit it is forfaiting
Factoring vs bills discounting
Management of book debts against borrowing from a bank; client/factor/debtor against drawer/drawee/payee
Which statute applies — none, or the Negotiable Instruments Act?
Bills payable vs bills discounting
Bills payable is credit the buyer takes; bills discounting is cash the seller raises
Which side of the invoice are you on?
Bills discounting vs bills acceptance
In discounting the company draws on its buyer; in acceptance it draws on the bank
Who accepts the bill?
Cash credit vs bank overdraft
Cash credit is the continuous working-capital line; the overdraft is for urgent need and is callable at short notice
The right of recall
Cost of availing trade credit vs cost of not availing it
Four costs for availing (price, goodwill, managing, conditions); three for not availing (inflation, interest, inconvenience)
Read the preposition in the question
Nominal vs compounded cost of a lost discount
ICAI uses the second in Illustration 17
Spontaneous vs negotiated sources
Spontaneous arise from ordinary business transaction; negotiated must be asked for
Bank credit is never spontaneous, and §6.2 excludes it from current liabilities
§3's nine factors vs §4.2's five factors
Nine for planning the requirement; five for deciding the level of investment
'Planning' against 'level of investment'

Each asset at the cost that has reached it, then current liabilities, then the margin

Stocks rise less than proportionately, WIP is unchanged, fixed cost per unit halves
What is the minimum cash balance to meet obligations?
Cash cycle (SM Illustration 11)
Annual outlay ÷ cash turnover, where the outlay is sales less net profit
What is the optimum cash balance?

C = √(2UP ÷ S), with U and S on the same time basis
How should cash be managed when flows are random?
Miller-Orr (§11.2)
h, z and zero; transfer h − z at the upper limit
Prepare a cash budget
Opening, receipts, payments, balance before adjustment, borrow or invest, closing
What is the surplus or deficit against a target balance?
§10.1, cumulative layout
The carry-forward makes the peak requirement visible

Expected profit, less the opportunity cost of receivables, equals net benefit

cases.title: Integrated Case 1 — Konark Ceramics Ltd. prepares a bank proposal, and then checks it against the operating cycle
facts: Konark Ceramics Ltd. is applying to its bank for a working capital limit and has asked you to prepare the proposal on a cash cost basis.
Annual sales are ₹72,00,000, all on credit, with two months allowed to customers. The company sells at a gross profit of 20% on sales.

Annual costs are: materials consumed ₹18,00,000, with two months' credit from suppliers; wages ₹14,40,000, with a one-month lag in payment; cash manufacturing expenses ₹10,80,000, paid one month in arrear; administrative expenses ₹5,40,000, paid one month in arrear; and selling expenses ₹4,20,000, paid quarterly in advance.
Depreciation of ₹4,80,000 is treated as part of the cost of production but is to be ignored on a cash cost basis.
The company holds one month's stock each of raw materials and finished goods, and keeps a cash balance of ₹2,00,000. Work-in-progress is to be ignored.
A safety margin of 10% is to be added. Assume 360 days, and that purchases equal consumption because stock levels are stable.

questions.q: The annual cash cost of production and the annual cash cost of sales are respectively:
reasoning: **Cash cost of production** = materials + wages + **cash** manufacturing expenses = ₹18,00,000 + ₹14,40,000 + ₹10,80,000 = ==**₹43,20,000**==. *Depreciation is excluded: SM §6.3 says non-cash costs are taken out because the funds actually blocked are only the cash costs.*
**Cash cost of sales** = cash cost of production + administrative + selling = ₹43,20,000 + ₹5,40,000 + ₹4,20,000 = ==**₹52,80,000**==.

==**The five-second check ICAI itself builds into Illustration 4.** Add back the depreciation of ₹4,80,000 to reach a **total cost of sales of ₹57,60,000**, which is **80% of sales of ₹72,00,000** — exactly the 20% gross profit the question states. ==If that reconciliation fails, a cost line has been misplaced before any current asset has been computed.**==

==Option B gives the figures **including depreciation** — ₹48,00,000 and ₹57,60,000 — which is the single commonest error in this question type. Option C mixes the two bases: a cash cost of production with a total cost of sales.==

questions.q: The gross working capital on a cash cost basis is:
reasoning: **Finished goods** = **cash cost of production** ₹43,20,000 × 1/12 = **₹3,60,000**. *Production, not sales — the goods are still in the warehouse and have not borne administrative or selling costs.*
**Debtors** = **cash cost of sales** ₹52,80,000 × 2/12 = **₹8,80,000**. *Sales, not production — and at cost, not at the ₹12,00,000 that two months of sales value would give.*
**Selling expenses paid in advance** = ₹4,20,000 × 3/12 = **₹1,05,000**. *Paid **quarterly in advance**, so three months sit as a **current asset**, not as a liability.*
**Cash balance** = **₹2,00,000**, as given.

==Option C, ₹19,15,000, is what results from valuing debtors at the sales figure of ₹12,00,000 less the prepayment treatment — the two errors §6.3 exists to prevent. Option D is the **net** figure, offered to catch a candidate who reads past the word 'gross'.==

==**One structural point worth carrying.** Of the ₹16,95,000, **debtors alone are ₹8,80,000 — 52% of the gross requirement.** In almost every official question in this chapter the debtors line is the largest single asset, which is why Unit IV carries more marks than Units I and II together.==

questions.q: The total working capital requirement to be put in the bank proposal, after the safety margin, is:
reasoning: **Current liabilities.** Creditors ₹18,00,000 × 2/12 = **₹3,00,000**; outstanding wages ₹14,40,000 × 1/12 = **₹1,20,000**; outstanding manufacturing expenses ₹10,80,000 × 1/12 = **₹90,000**; outstanding administrative expenses ₹5,40,000 × 1/12 = **₹45,000**. **Total = ₹5,55,000.**
**Add the safety margin at 10%** = ₹1,14,000. **Total Working Capital requirement = ==₹12,54,000==.**

==**Why 10% here is a mark-up and not a gross-up.** The question says simply **'a safety margin of 10% is to be added'**, with no 'inclusive of the margin' — so it is ₹11,40,000 × 1.10. Option D, ₹12,66,667, is the **gross-up** answer ₹11,40,000 ÷ 0.90, which MTP January 2025 Series II's wording would have required. ==**The two readings differ by ₹12,667 on these figures, and the only clue is whether the word 'inclusive' appears.**==

==Option B, ₹18,64,500, applies the margin to the **gross** working capital instead of the net — a slip that is easy to make if the statement is not laid out with Net Working Capital as a visible subtotal.==

**One note to write into the proposal.** The selling expenses prepayment of ₹1,05,000 is the only item in the statement on the **asset** side that arises from an expense, and it is there because the payment is made **in advance**. ==Every other expense in this question is paid **in arrear** and so reduces the requirement. Reading the direction of each lag — 'in advance' is an asset, 'in arrear' is a liability — is worth more in this question than any single calculation.==

questions.q: Checking the same figures by the operating cycle method, the net operating cycle and the number of cycles in the year are:
reasoning: **R** = average raw material ÷ consumption per day = ₹1,50,000 ÷ (₹18,00,000 ÷ 360) = ₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹5,000 = **30 days**.
**W** = **nil**, since work-in-progress is to be ignored.
**F** = average finished goods ÷ cost of goods sold per day = ₹3,60,000 ÷ (₹43,20,000 ÷ 360) = ₹3,60,000 ÷ ₹12,000 = **30 days**.
**D** = average debtors ÷ credit sales per day, on the cash cost basis used throughout = ₹8,80,000 ÷ (₹52,80,000 ÷ 360) = ₹8,80,000 ÷ ₹14,666.67 = **60 days**.
**C** = average creditors ÷ credit purchases per day = ₹3,00,000 ÷ (₹18,00,000 ÷ 360) = **60 days**.
**Net operating cycle** = 30 + 0 + 30 + 60 − 60 = ==**60 days**==, and the **number of cycles** = 360 ÷ 60 = ==**6 times**==.

==**And now the point of the question, which is the most useful idea in Unit I.** Working capital by the operating cycle method = annual operating cost ÷ number of cycles = **₹52,80,000 ÷ 6 = ₹8,80,000** — against the **₹11,40,000** the component statement produced. **The two methods disagree by ₹2,60,000, and both are right.**==

==**Why they differ.** The operating cycle method nets off **only the creditors' period**; the component statement also deducts the **accruals on wages, manufacturing and administrative expenses (₹2,55,000)** and adds the **cash balance (₹2,00,000)** and the **prepayment (₹1,05,000)**, none of which appears anywhere in R + W + F + D − C. **₹8,80,000 − ₹2,55,000 + ₹2,00,000 + ₹1,05,000 = ₹11,30,000**, within rounding of the statement figure. ==**The cycle method is a quick estimate built from inventory, debtors and creditors alone; the component statement is the complete one, and it is what a bank is given.**==

**Which to quote if a question asks for both.** Give the component figure as the requirement and the cycle as the diagnostic, and say in one line why they differ. ==SM §5 itself calls the operating cycle **'one of the most reliable methods'** — not the only one, and not the most complete.==

cases.trap: Question 1 hides depreciation inside the manufacturing figure; question 2 rewards knowing that finished goods take production cost and debtors take cost of sales, and that a prepayment is an asset; question 3 turns on whether 'a safety margin of 10%' is a mark-up or a gross-up; and question 4 is there to show that the two estimation methods are not expected to agree.

cases.title: Integrated Case 2 — Vindhya Auto Components Ltd. weighs a factor's offer
facts: Vindhya Auto Components Ltd. has annual credit sales of ₹5,40,00,000 and an average collection period of 72 days. Bad debts run at 1.25% of credit sales.
The company spends ₹6,00,000 a year on credit administration, of which 70% would be avoidable if the function were outsourced.

A factor has offered to purchase the receivables on a non-recourse basis. Its terms are: a commission of 1.5%, an advance of 85% of receivables after withholding 15% as a reserve, and interest at 16% per annum for the collection period.
The factor undertakes to bring the average collection period down to 60 days.
Vindhya's own cost of short-term borrowing is 13% per annum. Assume 360 days in a year.

questions.q: The average level of receivables before the factoring arrangement, and the level the factor's collection period would produce, are:
reasoning: **Present receivables** = credit sales × collection period ÷ 360 = ₹5,40,00,000 × 72 ÷ 360 = ==**₹1,08,00,000**==.
**After factoring**, at the guaranteed 60 days = ₹5,40,00,000 × 60 ÷ 360 = ==**₹90,00,000**==.

==**Which figure the rest of the computation uses, and this is the decision that governs the whole case.** The **₹90,00,000** is the base for the factor's commission, reserve and interest, because that is the book the factor will actually be managing. The **₹1,08,00,000** is used only once — to size the **interest saved** on the 12 days of collection the factor removes.==

**ICAI's precedent.** May 2024's Bright Ltd works exactly this way: the factor guarantees 45 days against an actual 70, and ICAI computes the average level of receivables on **45 days** while valuing the 25-day improvement as a separate saving.
==Option B reverses the two, and option D computes the present receivables on an 86-day period. **The arithmetic here is trivial; the sequencing is not.**==

questions.q: The total annual savings on taking the factoring service are:
reasoning: **All three of ICAI's savings lines are live in this question, which is what makes the offer worth taking.**
**Cost of credit administration saved** = 70% × ₹6,00,000 = ==**₹4,20,000**==. *Only the avoidable portion; the other 30% continues whether or not the factor is appointed.*

**Bad debts avoided** = 1.25% × ₹5,40,00,000 = ==**₹6,75,000**==. *The arrangement is **non-recourse**, so the whole bad-debt loss passes to the factor — contrast MTP September 2024 Series II's Sukrut Limited, where a **recourse** basis cut bad debts only from 1% to 0.5% and the saving was half the figure.*

**Interest saved due to the reduction in the average collection period** = cost of annual credit sales × rate of interest × (present collection period − new collection period) ÷ 360 = ₹5,40,00,000 × 13% × (72 − 60) ÷ 360 = ₹5,40,00,000 × 0.13 × 12/360 = ==**₹2,34,000**==. *Valued at **Vindhya's own 13%**, because the funds released are funds it no longer has to borrow.*

==Option A omits the interest saved, option B gives the bad debts alone, and option C charges the **whole** ₹6,00,000 of administration cost as a saving. **Each distractor drops exactly one of the three lines, which is how a well-built factoring MCQ is constructed** — and it is why the savings block should be written out as three labelled lines rather than a single total.==

questions.q: The amount available for advance, and the advance the factor will actually pay, are:
reasoning: **Start from the post-factoring receivables of ₹90,00,000 and work down ICAI's five steps.**
**Less the factor's interest at 16% for the 60-day collection period** = ₹75,15,000 × 0.16 × 60/360 = ₹75,15,000 × 0.026667 = **₹2,00,400**.

==**The distinction options C and D are built around.** ICAI's format states it in terms: **'Advances to be paid = (Amount available for advance − Interest deducted by factor).'** ==**Option C stops at step 4**, which is the error MTP September 2025 Series I's MCQ (vii) exists to catch — there option (a) ₹1,32,00,000 was the amount available and the answer was ₹1,26,06,000. **Option D deducts only the reserve and calls 85% of receivables the advance**, ignoring both the commission and the interest.==

**The shortcut for the interest step.** 16% for 60 days on a 360-day year is exactly **16% ÷ 6 = 2.667%**, so the advance is **97.333%** of the amount available. ==Any factoring question reduces the last step to one multiplication once the rate and the period are turned into a single percentage.==

questions.q: The effective cost of factoring, and the advice to Vindhya, are:

options.A: 9.09% and reject, since the company can borrow at 13%
options.B: 9.34% and accept, since the effective cost is below the company's 13% cost of borrowing
options.D: 9.34% and reject, since factoring always costs more than bank finance

reasoning: **The annual cost of factoring.** **Commission** = 1.5% × ₹5,40,00,000 = **₹8,10,000** *(annualised on credit sales, per ICAI's format)*. **Interest charged by the factor**, annualised = ₹75,15,000 × 16% = **₹12,02,400**. **Total cost = ₹20,12,400.**
**Rate of effective cost of factoring** = Net annual cost ÷ Advance to be paid × 100 = ₹6,83,400 ÷ ₹73,14,600 × 100 = ==**9.34%**==.

==**The advice.** ICAI's rule is explicit: **'The company should avail Factoring services if rate of effective Cost of Factoring to the firm is less than the existing cost of borrowing.'** At **9.34% against a cost of borrowing of 13%**, the offer is **cheaper than the money it replaces**, so ==**Vindhya should accept the factoring proposal**==.==

==**Why this offer passes where most official ones fail, and it is the lesson of the whole case.** The three published 2/40-net-120 questions all **reject**, with effective costs of 13.42% and 16.09%, because their factors do **nothing** to the collection period and their savings come to only ₹4,00,000–₹4,80,000. Vindhya's factor **shortens collection by 12 days** and takes the bad debts on a **non-recourse** basis, so all three savings lines fire and together they cover two-thirds of the cost. ==**A factoring proposal is won or lost on whether the factor improves the collection period and absorbs the credit risk — not on the commission rate.**==

==Option A, 9.09%, is the figure obtained by using the **amount available for advance** (₹75,15,000) as the denominator instead of the advance paid. **That denominator is itself acceptable — RTP September 2026 offers both — but the paired advice is wrong**, which is what makes the option a trap rather than a second right answer. **Option D has the arithmetic right and the conclusion backwards**, and the reason given is simply untrue.==

**One sentence to add in a descriptive version of this question.** The ₹1,35,000 commission deducted in computing the advance and the ₹8,10,000 charged as the annual cost are the **same 1.5% on two different bases** — receivables and credit sales. ==ICAI's own format permits both (**'Annual credit Sales × % of Commission (or calculated annually)'**), and January 2026's X Ltd answer uses both in one solution. Say which basis each figure uses and the point cannot be marked against you.==

cases.trap: Question 1 decides which receivables figure drives the rest; question 2 pays for all three savings lines, and each distractor drops exactly one; question 3 separates the amount available from the advance actually paid; and question 4 rewards knowing ICAI's decision rule rather than a general prejudice about factoring.

mcqs.question: The operating cycle of a firm is correctly expressed as:

options.A: R + W + F + D − C, where C is the credit period allowed by suppliers

mcqs.explanation: SM §6: Operating Cycle = R + W + F + D − C, where R is the raw material storage period, W the work-in-progress holding period, F the finished goods storage period, D the receivables collection period and C the credit period allowed by suppliers. C is the only subtraction, because supplier credit is the one stage that funds the cycle rather than consuming funds.

mcqs.question: On a cash cost basis, finished goods and debtors are valued respectively at:

options.A: The cash cost of production and the cash cost of sales
options.B: The cash cost of sales and the cash cost of production
options.C: The cash cost of production and the sales value
options.D: The total cost of production including depreciation, and the cash cost of sales

mcqs.explanation: SM §6.2 and §6.3: only cash cost is considered for debtors and finished goods, because sales to debtors include cost and profit whereas working capital need not fund the profit, and depreciation is excluded as a non-cash expense. Finished goods have not yet borne administrative and selling costs, so they take the cost of production; debtors have, so they take the cost of sales.

mcqs.question: A firm's total cash disbursements are ₹24,00,000 a year, the cost per transfer is ₹30 and marketable securities yield 12% per annum. Its optimum cash balance under Baumol's model is:
mcqs.explanation: C = √(2UP ÷ S) = √(2 × ₹24,00,000 × ₹30 ÷ 0.12) = √(₹14,40,00,000 ÷ 0.12) = √₹12,00,00,00,000 = ₹34,641. Option C omits the 2 and the division by S in the wrong order; option D is the annual disbursement divided by 20. The carrying cost of the balance is the interest forgone on marketable securities, and the transaction cost is the clerical, brokerage and registration cost of converting them into cash.

mcqs.question: The period between the sale and the mailing of the invoice is known as:
mcqs.explanation: SM §10.4 defines four floats: billing float is the time between the sale and the mailing of the invoice; mail float is the cheque in transit; cheque processing float is the time taken by the seller to sort, record and deposit the cheque; and banking processing float runs from deposit to the crediting of funds. A firm attacks the billing float simply by issuing invoices quickly.

mcqs.question: Under the Total Approach to evaluating credit policies, the fixed cost used in each proposed policy's column is:

options.A: Scaled in proportion to that policy's sales
options.B: The amount computed from the present policy's volume, held constant across all policies
options.C: Excluded altogether, since fixed costs are irrelevant to a credit decision
options.D: Replaced by the opportunity cost of investment in receivables

mcqs.explanation: SM §19: Total Fixed Cost = [Average cost per unit − Variable cost per unit] × number of units sold on credit under the Present Policy, and that figure is carried unchanged into every column. September 2024's AB Enterprises keeps fixed cost at ₹5,00,000 while units rise from 30,000 to 33,000 to 35,000 — scaling it with sales would turn a fixed cost into a variable one and destroy the comparison.

mcqs.question: Commercial paper may be issued for a maturity period of:

options.A: A minimum of 15 days to a maximum of 3 years
options.B: A minimum of 7 days to less than 1 year from the date of issue
options.C: Overnight to 1 year, at freely negotiable rates
options.D: Any period, provided the issuer is a highly rated corporate borrower

mcqs.explanation: SM §27.3: 'The maturity period ranges from minimum 7 days to less than 1 year from the date of issue. CP can be issued in denomination of ₹5 lakhs or multiples thereof.' Option C describes the range of money-market deposits in §12.3, which run from overnight to one year — a different instrument in a different section.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is true of forfaiting but **not** of factoring?

options.A: It converts receivables into immediate cash
options.B: It may be arranged either with or without recourse to the client
options.C: It is always without recourse and is confined to export trade bills
options.D: It includes administration of the client's sales ledger

mcqs.explanation: SM §20.2: forfaiting is finance provided to exporters 'without recourse basis in which risk and rewards related with the bills/receivables transferred to the financial institutions/banks', and it applies to trade bills from the export of goods or services. Factoring may be with or without recourse (option B) and includes sales-ledger administration (option D); both convert receivables into cash (option A).

mcqs.question: A working capital statement shows an excess of current assets over current liabilities of ₹24,00,000. A safety margin is to be kept at 20% of the net working capital required **inclusive of the margin amount**. The total net working capital is:
mcqs.explanation: 'Inclusive of the margin' means the computed excess is 80% of the answer, so net working capital = ₹24,00,000 ÷ 0.80 = ₹30,00,000 and the margin is ₹6,00,000. Option A adds a flat 20%, which is what a margin stated simply as '20%' would require — RTP September 2024 applies the gross-up as ₹4,49,792 × 1/9 for a 10% margin inclusive of itself, and MTP January 2025 Series II divides by 0.85 for a 15% one.

mcqs.question: Which of the following forms of bank credit is non-fund-based, in that the bank lends its creditworthiness rather than its money?
mcqs.explanation: SM §29: a letter of credit is 'an arrangement by which the issuing bank on the instructions of a customer or on its own behalf undertakes to pay or accept or negotiate or authorizes another bank to do so against stipulated documents' — the bank advances nothing unless the customer fails. Bills acceptance and bank guarantees are non-fund-based for the same reason. Cash credit, bills discounting and the overdraft all put funds in the borrower's hands.

mcqs.question: A supplier offers terms of 3/15, net 60. Using the study material's formula for the cost of the lost cash discount, the annualised cost of not taking the discount is approximately:
mcqs.explanation: t = 60 − 15 = 45 days, and the compounded formula is [100 ÷ (100 − d)]^(365/t) − 1 = [100/97]^(365/45) − 1 = [1.030928]^8.111 − 1 = 28.0%. Option B is the nominal form, 3/97 × 365/45 = 25.1% — ICAI says the nominal formula 'does not take into account the compounding effect and therefore, the cost of credit shall be even higher', which is exactly the gap between 25.1% and 28.0%. Option A is the error SM Illustration 18 exists to expose: comparing a discount percentage directly with an annual rate.

mcqs.question: The Miller-Orr cash management model differs from Baumol's model principally in that it:

options.A: Minimises the sum of carrying costs and transaction costs, which Baumol does not
options.B: Applies only where the firm holds no marketable securities
options.C: Requires the cash balance to be returned to zero whenever the upper limit is reached
options.D: Treats the net cash flow as completely stochastic and sets control limits rather than a single optimum balance

mcqs.explanation: SM §11.2: 'According to this model the net cash flow is completely stochastic', and the model sets h as the upper limit, z as the return point and zero as the lower limit. Baumol's limitation, ICAI says, 'is that it does not allow the cash flows to fluctuate'. Option A describes what both models do; option C is wrong because the transfer at the upper limit is h − z, which leaves the balance at the return point.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a spontaneous source of working capital finance carrying neither an explicit nor an implicit cost?
mcqs.explanation: SM §27.1(c): 'The accrued expenses represent an interest free source of finance. There is no explicit or implicit cost associated with the accrued expenses.' Trade credit is also spontaneous and carries no explicit cost, but its implicit cost — the discount forgone — is what §24(a) calls 'a high implicit cost'. Commercial paper and bank overdrafts are negotiated sources carrying explicit interest.

descriptive.question: From the following information of Arcot Textiles Ltd. for the year ended 31 March 2026, calculate the net operating cycle period, the number of operating cycles in the year, and the amount of working capital required. Annual purchases of raw material (all credit) ₹14,40,000; annual cost of production ₹21,60,000; annual cost of goods sold ₹25,20,000; annual operating cost ₹28,80,000; annual sales (all credit) ₹36,00,000. Opening and closing balances: raw material ₹1,00,000 and ₹1,40,000; work-in-progress ₹80,000 and ₹1,00,000; finished goods ₹1,80,000 and ₹2,40,000; debtors ₹3,60,000 and ₹4,40,000; creditors ₹1,00,000 and ₹1,40,000. Assume 360 days in a year.
answer_points: **State the formula and the convention.** **Operating Cycle = R + W + F + D − C**; 360 days assumed.
**Derive the raw material consumed first**, because the question gives purchases, not consumption. **Consumed = Opening + Purchases − Closing** = ₹1,00,000 + ₹14,40,000 − ₹1,40,000 = **₹14,00,000**.
**(i) Net operating cycle** = 31 + 15 + 30 + 40 − 30 = **86 days**.
**(ii) Number of operating cycles** = 360 ÷ 86 = **4.186 times**.
**(iii) Working capital required** = annual operating cost ÷ number of cycles = ₹28,80,000 ÷ 4.186 = **₹6,87,996**, say **₹6,88,000**.

**Three points of technique to state.** **(a)** The denominator for R is **consumption**, which had to be derived; using purchases would give 30 days instead of 31. **(b)** The denominator for C is **purchases**, not consumption — the two differ here by ₹40,000. **(c)** The working capital is computed on the **annual operating cost of ₹28,80,000**, not on the cost of goods sold of ₹25,20,000, and the question gives both to test that.
keywords: R on consumption, C on purchases

descriptive.question: Mysore Pumps Ltd. is considering relaxing its credit policy. Its present annual credit sales are ₹60,00,000 with an accounts receivable turnover ratio of 6 times a year and bad debt losses of ₹90,000. Proposed Policy A would raise sales to ₹72,00,000 with a turnover ratio of 4 times and bad debts of ₹2,16,000; Proposed Policy B would raise sales to ₹80,00,000 with a turnover ratio of 3 times and bad debts of ₹4,00,000. Variable costs are 65% of the selling price and fixed costs are ₹8,00,000. The company requires a return of 18% on the investment in receivables. Assume 360 days in a year. Evaluate the policies by the Total Approach and recommend one.
answer_points: **Convert the turnover ratios into collection periods first.** 360 ÷ 6 = **60 days**; 360 ÷ 4 = **90 days**; 360 ÷ 3 = **120 days**.
**Recommendation.** **Proposed Policy A should be adopted, since the net benefits under this policy are higher than under the other policies.**

**The comment that earns the last mark.** Expected profit rises at every step — ₹12.10 lakhs to ₹15.04 lakhs to ₹16.00 lakhs — but **net benefit peaks at Policy A**. Between A and B the profit rises by ₹96,000 while the opportunity cost rises by ₹1,13,400, so the extra sales do not pay for the extra 30 days of credit.

**Two technique points.** **Fixed cost is held at ₹8,00,000 in every column**, computed once from the present policy; and the opportunity cost is taken on the **total cost of credit sales**, not on sales value — ICAI's own formula in §19.

descriptive.question: Explain the different kinds of float with reference to the management of cash, and describe the two decentralised collection systems a firm may use to reduce float time, including the rule for deciding whether to adopt them.
answer_points: **Open with the definition and the objective.** **'The term float is used to refer to the periods that affect cash as it moves through the different stages of the collection process.'** The twin objectives of managing cash flows are to **accelerate cash collections as much as possible** and to **decelerate or delay cash disbursements within permissible time frame.**

**The four floats, each defined by its two boundary events.**
**Billing float** — **'the time between the sale and the mailing of the invoice.'**
**Mail float** — **'the time when a cheque is being carried by post office, messenger service or other means of delivery.'**
**Cheque processing float** — **'the time required for the seller to sort, record and deposit the cheque after it has been received by the company.'**
**Banking processing float** — **'the time from the deposit of the cheque to the crediting of funds in the sellers' account.'**

**How each is attacked.** Issue invoices quickly to cut the **billing** float; reduce the lag between the customer paying and the cheque being collected to cut the **mail** float; and make funds available for the firm's use to cut the **processing** floats.

**Concentration Banking.** **'the company establishes a number of strategic collection centers in different regions instead of a single collection center at the head office.'** Payments are **deposited with the respective local banks, which transfer all surplus funds to the concentration bank of head office**, generally located at the headquarters. ICAI calls it **'one important and popular way of reducing the size of the float.'**

**Lock Box System.** **'The purpose of lock box system is to eliminate the time between the receipts of remittances by the company and deposited in the bank.'** The company **rents a local post-office box and authorises its bank at each location to pick up the remittances**; the bank **picks up the mail several times a day and deposits the cheques in the company's account**, sending a deposit slip and a list of payments. **'This procedure frees the company from handling and depositing the cheques.'** Its specific effect is that the **cheque processing float is eliminated**.

**The drawback.** **'The main drawback of lock box system is the cost of its operation … Since the cost is almost directly proportional to the number of cheques deposited, lock box arrangements are usually not profitable if the average remittance is small.'**

**The decision rule, which applies to both systems.** **'The appropriate rule for deciding whether or not to use a lock box system or for that matter, concentration banking, is simply to compare the added cost of the most efficient system with the marginal income that can be generated from the released funds. If costs are less than income, the system is profitable and if the system is not profitable, it is not worth undertaking.'**

**Close on the symmetry.** On the collection side float is to be destroyed; on the payment side it is to be created — **'availability of cash can be maximized by playing the float'**, by estimating accurately when cheques issued will be presented and holding only enough balance to honour those actually expected on that date.

descriptive.question: Discuss the costs of availing trade credit and the costs of not availing it, and explain how a firm should decide whether to take a cash discount offered by a supplier.
answer_points: **Open with ICAI's concession.** **'Normally it is considered that the trade credit does not carry any cost. However, it carries the following costs.'** Trade credit is a **spontaneous source of finance** that **arises from ordinary business transaction** and contributes **about one-third of total short-term requirements.**

**The four costs of availing trade credit.**
**(i) Price** — **'There is often a discount on the price that the firm undergoes when it uses trade credit, since it can take advantage of the discount only if it pays immediately. This discount can translate into a high implicit cost.'**
**(ii) Loss of goodwill** — **'If the credit is overstepped, suppliers may discriminate against delinquent customers if supplies become short'**, and the effect **'depends very much on the relative market strengths of the parties involved.'**
**(iii) Cost of managing** — **'administrative and accounting costs that would otherwise be incurred.'**
**(iv) Conditions** — suppliers may **'insist that for availing the credit facility the order should be of some minimum size or even on regular basis.'**

**The three costs of not availing it.**
**(i) Impact of inflation** — **'borrowers are favored over the lenders as they were better off to pay the fixed outstanding amount later than sooner'**, and later transactions will be at higher prices.
**(ii) Interest** — **'Trade credit is a type of interest free loan, therefore failure to avail this facility has an interest cost.'**
**(iii) Inconvenience** — to a supplier **'geared to the deferred payment.'**

**How to decide on a cash discount — the arithmetic.** Compute the annualised cost of **not** taking it. The nominal form is **d ÷ (100 − d) × 365 ÷ t**; ICAI notes this **'does not take into account the compounding effect'** and gives the better form **[100 ÷ (100 − d)]^(365 ÷ t) − 1**, where **d is the size of the discount and t is the reduction in the payment period necessary to obtain it.**

**Then compare it with the rate at which money can be had or placed.** On SM Illustration 17's terms of **2/10, net 45**, the cost of refusing is **23.5%**; because the company can earn **25%** on the cash retained, **'it is better for the company to refuse the discount, as return on cash retained is more than the saving on account of discount.'** Conversely, May 2026's B Ltd can borrow at **7% post-tax** against a discount worth **8.571% post-tax**, so it accepts.

**The t to use is a judgement.** It is the number of days **actually given up**: 35 days in Illustration 17, where the comparison is day 10 against day 45, but only **5 days** in Illustration 18, where the company already pays on day 15 — which is why the cost there reaches **149%**.

**And the conclusion if the discount cannot be taken.** SM Illustration 18(b): **'If the bank loan facility could not be available, then in this case the company should resort to utilise maximum credit period as possible. Therefore, payment should be made in 30 days to reduce the interest cost.'** Paying early **without** taking the discount is the worst of both outcomes.

descriptive.question: Explain the two broad categories into which working capital finance may be classified, the parameters that should guide a finance manager's choice of source, and the forms of bank credit available.
answer_points: **Start with the bifurcation, which governs everything else.** **'It is advisable that the finance manager bifurcate the working capital requirements between the permanent working capital and temporary working capital. The permanent working capital is always needed irrespective of sales fluctuation; hence it should be financed by the long-term sources such as debt and equity. On the contrary the temporary working capital may be financed by the short-term sources of finance.'**

**The two categories.** **Spontaneous sources** are **'those which naturally arise in the course of business operations'** — ICAI's examples are **trade credit, credit from employees and credit from suppliers of services.** **Negotiated sources** are **'those which have to be specifically negotiated with lenders say, commercial banks, financial institutions, general public etc.'**

**The three spontaneous sources.** **Trade credit**, contributing **about one-third of total short-term requirements**, and termed **'open account trade credit'** where no formality is required; **bills payable**, where the purchaser gives **a written promise to pay on demand or at a fixed future date**; and **accrued expenses**, a **'built in and an automatic source'** which **'represent an interest free source of finance'** with **'no explicit or implicit cost'.**

**The six parameters guiding the choice.** **(i) Cost factor; (ii) Impact on credit rating; (iii) Feasibility; (iv) Reliability; (v) Restrictions; and (vi) Hedging approach or matching approach i.e., Financing of assets with the same maturity as of assets.**

**The negotiated sources beyond banks.** **Inter-corporate loans and deposits**, at a rate **higher than the bank rate** depending on the borrower's financial soundness; **commercial paper**, an **unsecured promissory note** for **highly rated corporate borrowers**, with a maturity from **a minimum of 7 days to less than 1 year** in denominations of **₹5 lakhs or multiples**; **funds generated from operations**, being **profit and depreciation**; **public deposits**, for **well-established big companies with huge capital base**; **bills discounting** and the **Bill Rediscounting Scheme** of the RBI, effective from **1 November 1970**; and **factoring**.

**The forms of bank credit** (SM §29), **banks being 'the major suppliers of working capital credit'**: **cash credit** — a facility **'on continuous basis'** which the borrower may not exceed; **bank overdraft** — for **'urgent need of funds'**, easily repaid and **callable at short notice**; **bills discounting** — the seller discounts a buyer-accepted bill, the bank **earmarking a limit**; **bills acceptance** — the company **draws a bill on the bank**, which accepts it; **line of credit** — **'a commitment by a bank to lend a certain amount of funds on demand specifying the maximum amount'**; **letter of credit** — the bank **'undertakes to pay or accept or negotiate'** against stipulated documents; and **bank guarantees**, extended **'on behalf of their clients in favour of third parties'.**

**One line that shows understanding rather than recall.** Of the seven forms, **cash credit, overdraft, bills discounting and a drawn line of credit are fund-based**, while **bills acceptance, letter of credit and bank guarantee are non-fund-based** — the bank lends its name and pays only on default.

**And on assessment.** The **RBI withdrew the Maximum Permissible Bank Finance prescription in April 1997**; banks are **'now free to evolve, with the approval of their Boards, methods for assessing the working capital requirements of borrowers, within the prudential guidelines and exposure norms prescribed'**, subject still to the instructions on **directed credit** and **prohibition of credit**. The **Tandon and Chore Committees** laid the original foundations in this area.
keywords: accruals have no explicit or implicit cost
cost, credit rating, feasibility, reliability, restrictions, matching

descriptive.question: Explain the approaches of working capital investment, and the relationship between the current assets to fixed assets ratio and the return on total assets.
answer_points: **The three approaches, decided by organisational policy and the risk-return trade off.**

**Aggressive** — investment is kept at **minimal investment in current assets**: the entity **holds a lower level of inventory, follows a strict credit policy and keeps less cash balance.** The advantage is that **a lower level of funds is tied up, which results in lower financial costs**; the flip side is the **risk of stock-outs** and that **the organisation could not grow, which leads to lower utilisation of fixed assets and long-term debts**, so that **in the long run the firm may stay behind the competitors.** It **'would better suit a highly integrated organisation with efficient processes.'**

**Conservative** — the organisation **invests high capital in current assets**, keeping **inventory higher, credit policies liberal, and cash balance as high as to meet any current liabilities immediately.** Advantages: **higher sales volume, increased demand due to the liberal credit policy, and increased goodwill among suppliers due to payment in short time.** Disadvantages: **increased cost of capital, inventory obsolescence, higher risk of bad debts, and shortage of liquidity in the long run due to longer operating cycles.**
**Moderate** — in between, where **'a balance between the risk and return is maintained to gain more by using the funds in very efficient manner.'**

**ICAI's summary sentence.** **'A conservative policy implies greater liquidity and lower risk whereas an aggressive policy indicates higher risk and poor liquidity. Moderate current assets policy will fall in the middle … which most of the firms follow to strike an appropriate balance as per the requirements of their trade or industry.'** A firm **may follow a different policy at different times.**

**The ratio.** **'Dividing current assets by fixed assets gives current assets/fixed assets ratio. Assuming a constant level of fixed assets, a higher current assets/fixed assets ratio indicates a conservative current assets policy and a lower current assets/fixed assets ratio means an aggressive current assets policy.'**

**The relationship, with ICAI's own figures.** On SM Illustration 1 — sales ₹20,00,000, EBIT ₹2,00,000, fixed assets ₹5,00,000 — current assets of **₹5,00,000, ₹4,00,000 and ₹3,00,000** give returns on total assets of **20%, 22.22% and 25%** against CA/FA ratios of **1.00, 0.80 and 0.60**. ICAI concludes that the table **'reflects inverse relationship between Current Assets / Fixed Assets ratio and Return on Total Assets.'**

**Why that must be so, in one line.** With EBIT and fixed assets constant, holding more current assets enlarges the denominator of the return without touching the numerator. And ICAI adds that **'generally, current assets do not increase in direct proportion to output; current assets may increase at a decreasing rate with output'**, because **'as the output increases, the firm starts using its current asset more efficiently.'**

**Close on the objective.** **'In determining the optimum level of current assets, the firm should balance the profitability – solvency tangle by minimizing total costs – Cost of liquidity and cost of illiquidity.'**
keywords: highly integrated organisation with efficient processes
inventory obsolescence and longer operating cycles
cost of liquidity and cost of illiquidity

quick.q: State the operating cycle equation and name each term.
quick.a: Operating Cycle = R + W + F + D − C: raw material storage period, work-in-progress holding period, finished goods storage period, receivables collection period, less the credit period allowed by suppliers.

quick.q: How is the working capital requirement found from the cycle?
quick.a: Number of cycles = 360 or 365 ÷ cycle period; working capital = annual operating cost ÷ number of cycles.

quick.q: At what value do finished goods and debtors enter a cash-cost statement?
quick.a: Finished goods at the cash cost of production; debtors at the cash cost of sales. Profit and depreciation are excluded from both.

quick.q: State Baumol's formula and define each symbol.
quick.a: C = √(2UP ÷ S), where C is the optimum cash balance, U the annual or monthly cash disbursement, P the fixed cost per transaction and S the opportunity cost of one rupee for the same period.

quick.q: Name the three limits of the Miller-Orr model and the action at each.
quick.a: h the upper limit — invest h − z in marketable securities; z the return point; zero the lower limit — transfer from securities to cash. Between the limits, no transaction.

quick.q: Name the four kinds of float.
quick.a: Billing float, mail float, cheque processing float and banking processing float.

quick.q: State the opportunity cost formula used in credit policy evaluation.
quick.a: Total cost of credit sales × collection period (days) ÷ 365 or 360 × required rate of return ÷ 100.

quick.q: State the formula for the rate of effective cost of factoring.
quick.a: Net annual cost of factoring ÷ amount available for advance (or ÷ advances to be paid) × 100.

quick.q: Give the two formulae for the cost of a lost cash discount.
Name the seven forms of bank credit.
quick.a: Cash credit, bank overdraft, bills discounting, bills acceptance, line of credit, letter of credit and bank guarantees.

differentiate.q: Gross working capital vs net working capital
differentiate.a: Both measure the same balance sheet from the value point of view. Gross working capital is the firm's investment in current assets; net working capital is current assets less current liabilities. A positive net figure indicates the ability to pay short-term liabilities, a negative one the inability — though a retail business collecting in cash and paying in arrear may run on negative net working capital quite soundly, as RTP January 2025's Samvar Ltd does at ₹(5.9396) lakh a store.

differentiate.q: Aggressive vs conservative working capital investment
differentiate.a: Aggressive keeps current assets at a minimum — lower inventory, a strict credit policy, less cash — so less funding is tied up and financial costs are lower, but there is stock-out risk and growth is forgone, leaving lower utilisation of fixed assets and long-term debt. Conservative invests high in current assets, winning higher sales volume, demand from liberal credit and supplier goodwill, but paying an increased cost of capital and risking inventory obsolescence, bad debts and a longer operating cycle. Conservative means greater liquidity and lower risk; aggressive means higher risk and poor liquidity.

differentiate.q: Baumol's model vs the Miller-Orr model
differentiate.a: Both determine how much cash to hold and both balance the cost of holding cash against the cost of converting securities. Baumol is an inventory-type model assuming cash needs are known with certainty and used uniformly; it gives a single optimum C = √(2UP ÷ S), and its stated limitation is that it does not allow cash flows to fluctuate. Miller-Orr is a stochastic control-limit model: the net cash flow is completely random, and it sets h, z and zero, investing h − z at the upper limit and selling securities at the lower. The current Study Material gives no formula for Miller-Orr's limits.

Both convert receivables into cash before due date. Factoring is 'invoice factoring' — a sort of management of book debts, between client, factor and debtor, continuous over the whole sales ledger, with credit control and ledger administration included, and no specific Act applies. Bills discounting is 'invoice discounting' — a sort of borrowing from commercial banks, between drawer, drawee and payee, transaction by transaction with no service attached, and the Negotiable Instruments Act applies.

Both are non-loan ways of turning receivables into cash. Factoring covers domestic or export receivables, may be with or without recourse, runs as a continuing arrangement over the ledger, and bundles finance with credit control and sales-ledger administration. Forfaiting applies only to export trade bills, is always without recourse, works transaction by transaction usually under a letter of credit or other negotiable instrument, and provides finance alone. Exim Bank of India's Buyer's Credit is ICAI's example of forfaiting.

Both are short-term sources. Trade credit is spontaneous — it arises from ordinary business transaction, comes from the supplier, is unsecured and informal where it is 'open account', carries no explicit interest but a high implicit cost in the discount forgone, and is tied to the purchase cycle. A bank overdraft is negotiated with a commercial bank, is usually secured and limited, carries explicit interest on the amount drawn, can be drawn and repaid quickly for an urgent need, and is issued with a right to call it in at short notice. Trade credit funds about one-third of short-term requirements; §6.2 excludes bank credit from the current liabilities deducted in sizing the requirement.

Both are running bank limits the borrower may not exceed, and both charge interest on the drawn amount. Cash credit is given 'on continuous basis' and is the standard working-capital facility, normally secured against inventory and receivables. A bank overdraft is 'made available to the companies in case of urgent need of funds', can be repaid 'quickly and easily' when no longer needed, and is issued with a right of recall at short notice — which is the operative distinction.

differentiate.q: Total Approach vs Incremental Approach to credit policy evaluation
differentiate.a: Both reach the same decision and both end in a net benefit compared across policies. The Total Approach states every policy in levels — credit sales, variable and fixed costs, bad debts, cash discount, tax, then the opportunity cost of receivables — and ICAI uses it in seven of its eight published answers. The Incremental Approach states only the differences from the present policy and the required return on the incremental investment; it is quicker where one proposal is on the table but unforgiving, because nothing in the statement reveals the level it started from.

sections.title: Unit I — the requirement
points: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities; gross is the investment in current assets, net the difference
Permanent working capital is the minimum carried at all times, financed long term; temporary meets sales fluctuation, financed short term
Too much means idle funds and over capitalization; too little means the risk of insolvency and lost sales
Current ratio 2 and quick ratio 1 are thumb rules only — optimum depends on the particular circumstances of the specific situation
Nine planning factors: cash · inventory · receivables · short-term financing · nature of business · market and demand · technology · operating efficiency · price levels and forex
Three Es: economy in financing, efficiency in utilisation, effectiveness in achieving objectives
Five components in the trade-off: inventory, receivables, pre-paid expenses, cash, payables — the payables row reads the opposite way
Investment asks 'how much' (effectiveness); financing asks 'where from' (economy)
Aggressive / moderate / conservative; a higher CA/FA ratio is conservative, and the ratio moves inversely to return on total assets
Illustration 1: ₹5L / ₹4L / ₹3L of current assets → 20% / 22.22% / 25% and 1.00 / 0.80 / 0.60
Minimise total costs — the cost of liquidity plus the cost of illiquidity

sections.title: Unit I — estimating it
points: Three methods: current assets holding period (the operating cycle, 'one of the most reliable'), ratio of sales, ratio of fixed investments
Operating Cycle = R + W + F + D − C, and C is the only subtraction
R ÷ consumption · W ÷ cost of production · F ÷ cost of goods sold · D ÷ credit sales · C ÷ credit purchases, each per day
Cycles = 360 or 365 ÷ cycle; working capital = annual operating cost ÷ cycles; more cycles is better
Each current asset = units per period × the cost that has reached it × the holding period
Debtors and finished goods at cash cost — profit and depreciation are excluded
Prepayments are current assets; bank credit is never deducted as a current liability
Split WIP into material and conversion and apply the two completion percentages separately
Cash cost of production = material + wages + cash manufacturing; cash cost of sales adds administrative and selling
Double shift: stocks rise less than proportionately, WIP is unchanged, fixed cost per unit halves — Samreen needs ₹94,800 more

sections.title: Unit II — treasury and cash
points: Treasury management: planning, organizing and controlling funds and working capital for best use, liquidity, lower cost and less risk
Five tasks: cash management · currency management · fund management · banking · corporate finance
Keynes's three motives: transaction, speculative, precautionary
Cash budget — the most significant device; four purposes; three methods, of which receipts and payments is commonly used
Accruals and depreciation never enter a receipts-and-payments budget
Four floats: billing · mail · cheque processing · banking processing
Concentration banking shortens the mail float; the lock box eliminates the cheque processing float
Decide either by comparing added cost with the marginal income from released funds
Baumol: C = √(2UP ÷ S); carrying cost is interest forgone, transaction cost is clerical, brokerage and registration
Miller-Orr: net cash flow completely stochastic; h, z and zero; invest h − z at the top; no formula in the SM
Seven recent developments, ending in virtual banking — popular for speed, convenience and round-the-clock access
Marketable securities: safety, maturity, marketability — mainly treasury bills, bank deposits and inter-corporate deposits
Cash cycle = debtors + inventory − creditors; minimum cash = annual outlay ÷ cash turnover

sections.title: Units III to V — inventory, receivables, payables
points: Inventory: objectives similar to cash management; detail is in Paper 4 Chapter 2
Receivables management is trade credit management, and the objective is to optimise the return on investment
Three aspects: credit policy · credit analysis · control of receivable
Four costs: interest or opportunity cost · administrative · collection · defaulting
'3/15 net 60' — 3% off by day 15, otherwise pay by day 60
Seven factors determining credit policy, and a rising trend in costs depresses the investment
Total Approach: credit sales − variable − fixed − bad debts − discount − tax, then the opportunity cost of receivables
Fixed cost from the present policy, held constant; opportunity cost on cost of credit sales
Net benefit peaks before profit does — AB Enterprises's Policy A, ABC Pvt Ltd's Policy 1, Banu Limited's Option I
Factoring: receivables − commission − reserve = available; − interest = advance; effective cost = net cost ÷ advance
Three savings (administration, bad debts, interest on a shorter cycle) against two costs (commission, interest)
Accept if the effective cost is below the cost of borrowing — Bright Ltd 7.504% yes, X Ltd 17.307% no
Pledging is a loan and raises debt; factoring is a sale and does not; forfaiting is export-only and always without recourse
Monitoring: the average age of receivables, then the ageing schedule for closer control over individual accounts
Payables: four costs of availing trade credit, three of not availing it
Lost discount: nominal d ÷ (100 − d) × 365 ÷ t; compounded [100 ÷ (100 − d)]^(365/t) − 1 — 23.5% on 2/10 net 45
If you cannot take the discount, pay on the last day of the credit period

sections.title: Unit VI — financing it
points: Bifurcate permanent and temporary, and match the maturity of the source to the asset
Six parameters: cost · credit rating · feasibility · reliability · restrictions · the hedging or matching approach
Spontaneous: trade credit (about one-third of short-term needs), bills payable, accrued expenses
Accrued expenses have no explicit or implicit cost; trade credit has no explicit cost but a high implicit one
Commercial paper: unsecured promissory note, highly rated issuers, 7 days to less than 1 year, ₹5 lakhs or multiples
Five CP advantages and two limitations — no early redemption and no extension
Funds from operations = profit + depreciation; public deposits suit well-established big companies
Bill Rediscounting Scheme: RBI, from 1 November 1970, all licensed scheduled banks eligible
Factoring against bills discounting: management of book debts against borrowing; no specific Act against the Negotiable Instruments Act
MPBF withdrawn by the RBI in April 1997; banks set their own methods with Board approval; Tandon and Chore Committees
Seven forms of bank credit — four fund-based, three (bills acceptance, letter of credit, bank guarantee) non-fund-based
